content: Antivenoms must be made accessible to all individuals who require them. Enhancing procurement and distribution systems will help reduce stock shortages in rural areas, while improved surveillance will enable quicker identification of issues related to product quality and safety. National systems for drug procurement, distribution, and surveillance will be strengthened to address these challenges. Snakebite envenoming is underreported in most countries, both at national and sub-national levels. Improved data collection and analysis are critical for understanding the burden of the disease and for allocating resources effectively. A standardized approach, including common tools and applications, as well as clearly defined minimum data requirements, will be established to assess the impact of snakebite envenoming on health systems and communities. Support will be provided to health systems to enhance their capacity to collect, compile, and analyze data on snakebite envenoming. Snakebite envenoming should be integrated into national and sub-national health plans to meet Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and Universal Health Coverage (UHC) 2030 targets. In some regions, specific types of snakebite envenoming require additional resources due to their severe consequences, such as long-term renal injury caused by certain snake species. Addressing these needs will require significant investment in specialized care and medical supplies. National and sub-national programs tailored to specific needs should be supported with appropriate tools and resources. Enhanced monitoring and surveillance of the disease burden are essential. Including snakebite envenoming as a notifiable disease will facilitate the collection of accurate data for modeling the economic, health, and social impacts of the disease. Accurate estimates of the burden of snakebite envenoming at sub-national, national, regional, and global levels will help identify priority areas and resource requirements. Snakebite envenoming is significantly underreported, partly because many cases are not registered in health systems. The most reliable data come from both health systems and community-based sources. Standardized, comparable, and reliable data collection methods, tools, and applications will be developed to improve the quality of data. Robust surveillance systems will be established to collect, store, analyze, and report data on snakebite envenoming. Preclinical and clinical research on snakebite envenoming will be encouraged to improve understanding of the disease, its clinical outcomes, and the effectiveness of treatments. New testing procedures that reduce or eliminate the use of live animals in antivenom research will align with international commitments to ethical research practices. Investment in pragmatic, cost-effective clinical studies will provide evidence on the safety and efficacy of antivenoms and improve resource allocation by health ministries. The strategy emphasizes the importance of integrating snakebite envenoming into public health programs and national health plans. Countries will be supported with tools and resources to accelerate progress toward UHC 2030 and the SDGs, improving health outcomes for all. Advocacy and effective communication are critical for raising awareness and mobilizing resources to address snakebite envenoming. A comprehensive communication strategy will be developed, including core media materials and resources tailored to different contexts. Local partnerships and networks will be established to engage communities and promote prevention and risk mitigation strategies. Regional partnerships and alliances will be strengthened to address common challenges related to antivenom supply, production, and quality. WHO will work with countries to establish regional cooperation projects, improve antivenom production, and create stockpiles. Data management and analysis will be coordinated through the WHO Global Health Observatory, which will serve as a central repository for snakebite envenoming data. Standardized data will be regularly analyzed and published to inform evidence-based decision-making. The inclusion of snakebite envenoming in the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) will provide valuable data for understanding the etiology and outcomes of the disease. A strong investment case will be developed to secure adequate resources for the prevention and control of snakebite envenoming. This will involve robust data analysis and modeling to demonstrate the economic and health benefits of integrating snakebite envenoming control into health systems. Implementation research will highlight the benefits of integrating snakebite envenoming control with other NTDs and health initiatives, fostering new partnerships and collaborations. In summary, addressing snakebite envenoming requires a comprehensive strategy that includes improved access to antivenoms, enhanced surveillance, integration into health systems, robust research, and strong partnerships. These efforts will contribute to achieving UHC 2030 and the SDGs, ensuring better health outcomes for affected populations.
